{{Short description|Concept in mathematical analysis}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''Dirichlet kernel''', is the collection of periodic functions defined as

<math display="block">D_n(x)= \sum_{k=-n}^n e^{ikx} = 1+2\sum_{k=1}^n\cos(kx)=\frac{\sin\left(\left(n +1/2\right) x \right)}{\sin(x/2)},</math>

where {{mvar|n}} is any [[nonnegative integer]]. The kernel functions are periodic with period <math>2\pi</math>.

[[file:Dirichlet kernel anime.gif|thumb|300px|Plot restricted to one period <math>[-L,L],~L=\pi,~</math> of the first few Dirichlet kernels showing their convergence to one of the [[Dirac delta function|Dirac delta]] distributions of the [[Dirac comb]].]]

The importance of the Dirichlet kernel comes from its relation to [[Fourier series]]. The [[convolution]] of <math>D_n(x)</math> with any function <math>f</math> of period <math>2\pi</math> is the <math>n</math>th-degree Fourier series approximation to <math>f</math>, i.e., we have

<math display="block">(D_n*f)(x)=\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(y)D_n(x-y)\,dy=2\pi\sum_{k=-n}^n \hat{f}(k)e^{ikx},</math>

where

<math display="block">\widehat{f}(k)=\frac 1 {2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi f(y)e^{-iky}\,dy</math>

is the <math>k</math>th Fourier coefficient of <math>f</math>. This implies that in order to study convergence of Fourier series it is enough to study properties of the Dirichlet kernel.

The Dirichlet kernel was named for [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]].

==Applications==

In [[signal processing]], the Dirichlet kernel is often called the '''periodic sinc function''':

:<math> P(\omega) =  D_n(x)|_{x = 2 \pi \omega/\omega_0}  = { \sin(\pi M \omega / \omega_0 ) \over \sin(\pi \omega / \omega_0 ) } </math>

where <math>M = 2n + 1 \ge 3</math> is an odd integer. In this form, <math>\omega</math> is the [[angular frequency]], and <math>\omega_0</math> is half of the periodicity in frequency. In this case, the periodic [[sinc function]] in the [[frequency domain]] can be thought of as the Fourier transform of a time bounded impulse train in the [[time domain]]:

:<math>p(t) = \sum_{k=-n}^n \delta(t - kT)</math>

where <math>T = \frac{\pi}{\omega_0}</math> is the time increment between each impulse and <math>M = 2n+1</math> represents the number of impulses in the impulse train. 

This kernel is also the Fourier Transform of a discrete time [[moving average]] filter.

In [[optics]], the Dirichlet kernel is part of the mathematical description of the [[diffraction]] pattern formed when monochromatic light passes through an aperture with [[diffraction from slits|multiple narrow slits]] of equal width and equally spaced along an axis perpendicular to the optical axis.  In this case, <math>M</math> is the number of slits.

[[File:Dirichlet kernels.svg|thumb|300px|Plot restricted to one period of the first few Dirichlet kernels (multiplied by <math>2 \pi</math>).]]

=={{math|''L''{{sup|1}}}} norm of the kernel function==

Of particular importance is the fact that the [[Lp space|<math>L^1</math>]] norm of <math>D_n</math> on <math>[0, 2\pi]</math> diverges to infinity as <math>n\to\infty</math>. One can estimate that (using the [[Big_O_notation#The_Hardy–Littlewood_definition|big omega notation]])

<math display="block">\| D_n \| _{L^1} = \Omega(\log n). </math>

By using a Riemann-sum argument to estimate the contribution in the largest neighbourhood of zero in which <math>D_n</math> is positive, and [[Jensen's inequality]] for the remaining part, it is also possible to show that:

<math display="block">\| D_n \|_{L^1} \geq 4\operatorname{Si}(\pi)+\frac 8 \pi \log n</math>

where <math display="inline"> \operatorname{Si}(x)</math> is the [[sine integral]] <math display="inline"> \int_0^x (\sin t)/t\, dt. </math>

This lack of uniform integrability is behind many divergence phenomena for the Fourier series. For example, together with the [[uniform boundedness principle]], it can be used to show that the Fourier series of a [[continuous function]] may fail to converge pointwise, in rather dramatic fashion. See [[convergence of Fourier series]] for further details.

A precise proof of the first result that <math>\| D_n \| _{L^1[0,2\pi]} = \Omega(\log n)</math> is given by

<math display="block">\begin{align} 
\int_0^{2\pi} |D_n(x)| \, dx & \geq \int_0^\pi \frac{\left|\sin[(2n+1)x]\right|}{x} \, dx \\[5pt]
     & \geq \sum_{k=0}^{2n} \int_{k\pi}^{(k+1)\pi} \frac{\left|\sin s\right|}{s} \, ds \\[5pt]
     & \geq \left|\sum_{k=0}^{2n} \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin s}{(k+1)\pi} \, ds\right| \\[5pt]
     & = \frac{2}{\pi} H_{2n+1} \\[5pt]
     & \geq \frac{2}{\pi} \log(2n+1),
\end{align}
</math>

where we have used the [[Taylor series]] identity that <math>2/x \leq 1 / \left|\sin(x/2)\right|</math> and where <math>H_n</math> are the first-order [[harmonic number]]s.

==Relation to the periodic delta function==

The Dirichlet kernel is a [[periodic function]] which becomes the [[Dirac comb]], i.e. the periodic delta function, in the limit
:<math> \lim_{n \to \infty} D_n(\omega) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=-n}^{n} e^{\pm i \omega k} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\pm i 2 \pi k x} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(x- k)=2\pi \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(\omega - 2\pi k)  ~, </math> 
with the angular frequency <math>\omega=2 \pi x</math>.

This can be inferred from the autoconjugation property of the Dirichlet kernel under forward and inverse [[Fourier transform]]:
:<math>\mathcal{F}\left[ D_n(2 \pi x) \right](\xi) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[ D_n(2 \pi x) \right](\xi) =  \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} D_n(2 \pi x) e^{\pm  i 2\pi \xi x} \, dx = \sum_{k=-n}^{+n} \delta(\xi-k) \equiv \operatorname{comb}_n(\xi)</math>
:<math>\mathcal{F}\left[ \operatorname{comb}_n \right](x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left[ \operatorname{comb}_n \right](x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \operatorname{comb}_n(\xi) e^{ \pm i 2 \pi \xi x } \, d\xi = D_n(2 \pi x),</math>
and <math>\operatorname{comb}_n(x)</math> goes to the [[Dirac comb]] <math>\operatorname{\text{Ш}}</math> of period <math>T=1</math> as <math>n \rightarrow \infty</math>, which remains invariant under [[Dirac comb#Fourier transform|Fourier transform]]: <math>\mathcal{F}[\operatorname{\text{Ш}}]= \operatorname{\text{Ш}}</math>. Thus <math>D_n(2 \pi x)</math> must also have converged to <math>\operatorname{\text{Ш}}</math> as <math>n \rightarrow \infty</math>.

In a different vein, consider <math>\Delta(x)</math> as the [[identity element]] for convolution on functions of period <math>2\pi</math>. In other words, we have

<math display="block">f*( \Delta)=f </math>

for every function <math>f</math> of period&nbsp;2{{pi}}. The Fourier series representation of this "function" is

<math display="block">\Delta(x)\sim\sum_{k=-\infty}^\infty e^{ikx}= \left(1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^\infty \cos(kx)\right).</math>

(This Fourier series converges to the function almost nowhere.) Therefore, the Dirichlet kernel, which is just the sequence of partial sums of this series, can be thought of as an ''[[approximate identity]]''. Abstractly speaking it is not however an approximate identity of ''positive'' elements (hence the failures in [[pointwise convergence]] mentioned above).

==Proof of the trigonometric identity==

The [[trigonometric identity]]

<math display="block">\sum_{k=-n}^n e^{ikx} = \frac{\sin((n+1/2)x)}{\sin(x/2)}</math>

displayed at the top of this article may be established as follows.  First recall that the sum of a finite [[geometric series]] is

<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^n a r^k=a\frac{1-r^{n+1}}{1-r}.</math>

In particular, we have

<math display="block">\sum_{k=-n}^n r^k=r^{-n}\cdot\frac{1-r^{2n+1}}{1-r}.</math>

Multiply both the numerator and the denominator by <math>r^{-1/2}</math>, getting

<math display="block">\frac{r^{-n-1/2}}{r^{-1/2}}\cdot\frac{1-r^{2n+1}}{1-r} =\frac{r^{-n-1/2}-r^{n+1/2}}{r^{-1/2}-r^{1/2}}.</math>

In the case <math>r = e^{ix}</math> we have

<math display="block">\sum_{k=-n}^n e^{ikx} = \frac{e^{-(n+1/2)ix}-e^{(n+1/2)ix}}{e^{-ix/2}-e^{ix/2}} = \frac{-2i\sin((n+1/2)x)}{-2i\sin(x/2)} = \frac{\sin((n+1/2)x)}{\sin(x/2)}</math>

as required.

===Alternative proof of the trigonometric identity===

Start with the series

<math display="block"> f(x) = 1 + 2 \sum_{k=1}^n\cos(kx).</math>

Multiply both sides by <math display="inline">\sin(x/2)</math> and use the trigonometric identity

<math display="block">\cos(a)\sin(b) = \frac{\sin(a + b) - \sin(a - b)} 2</math>

to reduce the terms in the sum.

<math display="block"> \sin(x/2)f(x) = \sin(x/2)+ \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \sin((k + \tfrac 1 2 )x)- \sin((k-\tfrac 1 2 )x) \right)</math>

which [[telescoping series|telescopes]] down to the result.

== Variant of identity ==
If the sum is only over non-negative integers (which may arise when computing a [[discrete Fourier transform]] that is not centered), then using similar techniques we can show the following identity:

<math display="block">\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} e^{ikx} = e^{i(N-1)x/2}\frac{\sin(N \, x/2)}{\sin(x/2)}</math>

Another variant is 
:<math>D_n(x) - \cos (nx) = \frac{\sin\left(nx \right)}{\tan(\frac{x}{2})}</math> 

and this can be easily proved by using an identity <math>\sin (\alpha + \beta) = \sin (\alpha) \cos (\beta) + \cos (\alpha) \sin(\beta)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fay |first1=Temple H. |last2=Kloppers |first2=P. Hendrik |date=2001 |title=The Gibbs' phenomenon |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00207390117151 |journal=International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=73–89 |doi=10.1080/00207390117151|s2cid=120595055 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
